prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not correct the sodium by more than 8 mEq/L in any 24 hours: osmotic demyelination risk.
Do not use the ammonia level to grade HE or to guide treatment, and do not repeat it to monitor response (ACG 2026 recommendation 5).
required_recommendations: Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.

Identify and treat the precipitants: relieve the 5-day constipation with lactulose and correct the hypokalemia and hyponatremia caused by the diuretic regimen (furosemide continued while spironolactone was taken irregularly).

Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis; stop the diuretics while overt HE, hypokalemia and hyponatremia persist, and restart a spironolactone-based regimen once they resolve (EASL 2018).
Correct sodium slowly, by no more than 8 mEq/L in any 24 hours (high osmotic demyelination risk with cirrhosis, hypokalemia and poor intake); potassium replacement also raises the serum sodium.
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid (a week of poor intake in cirrhosis).
Stop metformin (decompensated, Child-Pugh C cirrhosis: risk of lactic acidosis) and manage glucose with insulin.
After recovery, continue lactulose as secondary prophylaxis after this first overt episode; add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily only if overt HE recurs (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Start primary prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (norfloxacin 400 mg daily, or ciprofloxacin): ascitic total protein 1.2 g/dL with Child-Pugh 12, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL and sodium 128 mEq/L (EASL 2018).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 26 (EASL 2018).
Advise him not to drive (he is a truck driver) until recovery is confirmed and reassessed by his hepatologist.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 26), precipitated by hypokalemia (K 3.2; furosemide continued while spironolactone was taken irregularly) and constipation (5 days), with hyponatremia (Na 128) as a co-precipitant.

differential.diagnosis: Hyponatremic encephalopathy as the sole cause
differential.key_features: Na 128 mEq/L is a co-precipitant, but symptomatic hyponatremic encephalopathy usually needs lower values and does not explain the asterixis and sleep-wake reversal; correct slowly while treating HE.
Ascites present, but ascitic PMN 82 cells/mm3 (below 250) with no organisms and no growth; afebrile, WBC 8.2, CRP normal.

Confusion and a wide-based gait after a week of poor intake, but no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus and no alcohol use; asterixis and clear metabolic precipitants point to HE. Empirical parenteral thiamine covers it.
EEG shows generalized slowing with atypical triphasic-like waves but no epileptiform discharges and no electrographic seizures.
Platelets 88 and INR 1.8 raise the risk, but there is no focal deficit or trauma and CT shows no hemorrhage.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh C (12: bilirubin 3.8 3, albumin 2.4 3, INR 1.8 2, mild ascites 2, HE grade II 2); MELD-Na 26 (creatinine 1.2, bilirubin 3.8, INR 1.8, sodium 128).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration and renal failure.
Hypokalemia promotes renal ammoniagenesis by increasing glutamine extraction in the proximal tubule, an under-recognized but common HE precipitant.

EEG triphasic waves are non-specific (any metabolic encephalopathy); their absence does not rule out HE, and atypical morphology should not deflect the diagnosis, although it is a reason to exclude NCSE on the EEG itself.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Na 128 is a co-precipitant but too mild to explain the picture alone; asterixis, the sleep-wake reversal and the precipitants (hypokalemia, constipation) in decompensated cirrhosis make HE the primary diagnosis. Correct sodium slowly; treat HE.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose hyponatremic encephalopathy as primary and pursue aggressive sodium correction.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Classic triphasic waves are not required for HE and are non-specific; the recording shows diffuse slowing with no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures, which argues against NCSE without any drug challenge.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss HE because EEG is not 'classic'.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. V. is a 52-year-old man with NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14 at his last hepatology clinic review) who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for 2 days of worsening confusion, difficulty finding words, and increasing irritability. He had been increasingly forgetful over the prior month but the acute worsening began 48 hours ago. His wife noted he could not remember conversations from hours before, was not tracking time, and had been sleeping more than usual during the day while being restless at night — a reversal of his normal sleep pattern. He did not report dark stools, hematemesis, or abdominal pain. His wife reported that he had been constipated for approximately 5 days and had not been taking his spironolactone regularly due to dizziness when standing. He denied alcohol use. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal distension and decreased appetite over the prior week. He had no prior episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. He denied fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia. He had no focal weakness or sensory changes. His medications were reviewed and no new medications had been added.
